ii-agenty-dlya-biznesa.title: AI agents for business: what you can trust them with today
ii-agenty-dlya-biznesa.excerpt: How an agent differs from a chatbot, which tasks companies already hand over to one, why a model makes mistakes with confidence and how to catch them, what to do about personal data — and what a rollout costs.
ii-agenty-dlya-biznesa.lead: A year ago, AI in a company meant a chat window that employees pasted emails into. Today it increasingly means an agent that reads an enquiry by itself, finds the answer in the knowledge base, creates a deal in the CRM and calls in a person when it isn't sure. Here we look at what such an agent can really be trusted with, where it gets things wrong, how it works under the hood and what bringing one in costs.
ii-agenty-dlya-biznesa.metaTitle: AI agents for business: tasks, risks and costs
ii-agenty-dlya-biznesa.metaDescription: What an AI agent is and how it differs from a chatbot, which tasks it takes on, how to handle model errors, what 152-FZ requires and what a rollout costs.

sections.heading: Agent, assistant, chatbot: what's the difference
body: An ordinary chatbot follows a script: buttons, branches, answers written in advance. It doesn't understand a question that doesn't match any of the buttons, and honestly replies "I didn't understand".

An assistant built on a language model understands free text and answers in its own words. But it only answers: it does nothing in your systems, which means all the work after the answer is still left to a person.

An agent is the next step. It is given tools: find an order by its number, check what is left in stock, create a deal in the CRM, book a client into a free slot. The model decides for itself which tool to call and in what order, gets the result and carries on until the task is done or until it is time to call in a person.

For a business, the difference is fundamental. An assistant saves time on wording an answer. An agent closes the whole enquiry — and that is exactly why an agent's mistake costs more: it didn't just give an inaccurate answer, it did something.

sections.heading: What companies already hand over to an agent
body: First-line support. Opening hours, delivery terms, order status, returns, warranty — questions whose answers already sit in your documents and systems. The agent answers instantly, around the clock, and passes anything complicated to an employee with the context already gathered.

Sorting incoming messages. Emails, enquiries from the website, messenger messages: the agent works out what each one is — an order, a complaint, a question, spam — pulls out the contact details and the gist, creates a card in the CRM and sends it to the right department. A manager starts the day not by sorting the inbox but with a ready-made list of tasks.

Working with documents. Invoices, contracts, completion certificates, specifications: the agent finds the fields it needs, checks the amounts against the invoice in the accounting system and flags any discrepancies. What used to be typed in by hand now only needs checking.

Helping sales. A draft commercial proposal from a brief, an answer to a typical objection, a short summary of the correspondence with a client before a call. The decision stays with the manager, but the blank page disappears.

Internal knowledge search. Policies, instructions, past projects: an employee asks in their own words and gets an answer with a link to the document. This is the most underrated scenario — it has no external customers, but it saves every new employee hours every week.

sections.heading: Where an agent still falls short
body: Where a mistake costs more than the savings. Decisions about money, legal wording, medical and financial advice — the agent can prepare a draft, but a person has to sign it off.

Where there is no data. The agent doesn't know your prices, lead times and exceptions until you give them to it. If the answer lives only in the head of an experienced manager, the agent will guess it — and guess plausibly.

Where every case is unique. A complex deal with negotiations, a conflict with a client, a non-standard order. An agent needs repetitive tasks: on rare ones it makes mistakes more often and brings less benefit.

And where there is no process. If enquiries get lost today because nobody is responsible for sorting them, an agent won't help — it will neatly file the enquiries away where nobody looks. Process first, automation second.

sections.heading: Why a model is confidently wrong
body: A language model doesn't look the answer up in a database — it continues the text in the most probable way. When it doesn't have the fact it needs, it fills in a plausible one: a tariff that doesn't exist, an invented delivery time, a contract clause that isn't there. And it says all this in the same confident tone as the truth.

The main cure is grounding. The agent answers not "from memory" but from the documents it has found: first a search of your knowledge base, then an answer based strictly on what was found, with a link to the source. If nothing turns up, the right answer is "I don't know, I'm passing this to a specialist", and that has to be written explicitly into the agent's instructions.

The second is narrow boundaries. An online shop's support agent has no business discussing politics or giving health advice. The more precisely you describe what it does and what it doesn't do, the less room there is for invention.

The third is verification wherever the answer is structured. If the agent has pulled the total and the tax ID (INN) from an invoice, they can be checked against the accounting system automatically. If it has filled in a card in the CRM, the required fields are checked by code, not by hope.
There will still be mistakes. The goal is not zero mistakes but mistakes that are rare, visible and cheap: ones that reach a person rather than a client.

sections.heading: Where an agent gets its knowledge
body: Most often, from your knowledge base: instructions, policies, price lists, answers to frequently asked questions, past correspondence. The documents are cut into fragments, and for each question the agent finds the most relevant pieces and answers from them. This approach is called RAG — retrieval-augmented generation.

Fine-tuning a model on your data is needed less often than it seems. It changes the style and manner, but it is poor at adding facts: prices and lead times that change every month still have to come from up-to-date documents. That is why almost every project starts with a search over the knowledge base and leaves fine-tuning for later — if it is needed at all.

An agent's answers cannot be better than its documents. An outdated price list in the base means an outdated price in the answer. Three versions of the same policy mean three different answers to one question. Putting the knowledge base in order often takes longer than the development itself, and that is normal.

The knowledge base needs an owner: someone who updates the documents when prices and terms change, and looks at which questions the agent couldn't find an answer to. Without that person, six months from now the agent will be politely recounting last year's terms.

sections.heading: Tools: how an agent acts rather than just answers
body: A tool is a function in your system that the agent is allowed to call: find an order, look up free slots, create a request, send a notification. The model sees a description of the tool, decides for itself when to call it and gets the result.

Every tool is a form of access. A support agent needs to read an order's status, but it doesn't need to change prices or delete clients. Permissions are granted at the minimum, exactly for the scenario — just as they are for a new employee on probation.

Irreversible actions require confirmation. Cancelling an order, issuing a refund, sending an email to every client — the agent prepares the action, a person presses the button. It is a little slower and gives you incomparably more peace of mind.

And everything the agent does is logged: which question came in, which tools were called, with which parameters, what the systems returned. Without such a log you can neither investigate a mistake nor prove that there wasn't one.

sections.heading: Human in the loop
body: A good agent knows when to stop. The rules for handing over to a person are written in advance: the client is unhappy, the question is about money, the agent hasn't found an answer, the client explicitly asks for an operator, the conversation is going round in circles.

A handover is not "I'm putting you through to an operator" followed by starting from scratch. The employee receives the enquiry with a summary: who the client is, what they asked, what the agent has already checked and why it stopped. The client doesn't have to explain everything all over again, and that is the main sign that automation has been built for people rather than instead of them.

At the start it helps to keep a person closer: for the first few weeks the agent prepares answers, and an employee checks and sends them. That way you can see where the agent goes wrong, and the knowledge base fills out quickly. Once the quality has settled, the review is kept only for risky topics.

It is worth bringing your employees into the project from the very start. The agent takes the routine off their hands rather than replacing them — and they are the ones who know best which questions keep coming up and where the exceptions are hiding.

sections.heading: Personal data and 152-FZ
body: As soon as an agent handles client enquiries, personal data passes through it: names, phone numbers, addresses, order history. The company remains the operator of that data and is responsible for it under Federal Law 152-FZ, Russia's personal data law, whoever processes it technically.

Sending data to a model run by a foreign service is a cross-border transfer of personal data: Roskomnadzor, Russia's data protection authority, has to be notified in advance, and the service itself must ensure the data is protected. For many companies it is simpler to choose a model from a Russian provider or to deploy an open model on their own server.

Whichever you choose, it is worth masking anything superfluous. A model doesn't need a passport number to answer a question about delivery: data the task can be solved without can be replaced with placeholders before sending and substituted back into the answer.

And a separate point: the logs. Conversations stored for quality control are personal data too. They need a clear retention period and a deletion rule, otherwise within a year the agent's log will become the largest and least protected client database in the company.

sections.heading: How to tell that an agent is working well
body: Before launch, you collect a set of real questions — fifty, a hundred, two hundred — with the correct answers. The agent is tested against it after every change: a new instruction, new documents, a switch of model. Without such an evaluation set, any improvement is a feeling, not a fact.

The metrics are simple. What share of enquiries is closed without a person. How accurate the answers are, judging by spot checks. How often the agent hands the conversation to an employee, and for what reasons. How long it takes to get an answer. And, separately, complaints about the agent's answers.

Quality doesn't stand still after launch. Prices change, new products appear, clients start asking about other things. The questions the agent couldn't find an answer to are the best list of what needs adding to the knowledge base this week.

Compare against how things were before the agent, not against the ideal. If an enquiry sent at the weekend used to get an answer on Monday, and now it gets one within a minute and a correct one nine times out of ten, that is a win — even if the tenth case goes to a person.

sections.heading: What a rollout costs
body: One scenario on one channel — for example, a first-line agent in Telegram that answers from the knowledge base and passes complicated cases to an employee — from {price:90000} and from two weeks. That includes setting it up for your documents, testing it on real questions and the launch.

Several scenarios with integration into the CRM and the knowledge base, quality monitoring and support after launch — from {price:180000} and from three weeks. This is the most common option: the agent not only answers but also creates deals, updates statuses and writes summaries for managers.

End-to-end automation — several connected agents, complex integrations with accounting systems, analytics — from {price:350000} and from five weeks. Here the timeline is most often set not by the agents but by the integrations and the state of the data.

Running costs are a separate line item. Calls to the model are paid for by volume, and at hundreds of enquiries a day this is a noticeable but predictable sum, which you can already see during the trial period. Your own model on your own server costs more at the start and less at high volumes — and, most importantly, the data goes nowhere.

sections.heading: Off-the-shelf service or custom development
body: Off-the-shelf services with an AI bot connect in a day: you upload your documents and get a widget for your website. For simple help on a website that is often enough, and there is no reason to pay for development.

The limitations begin where the agent needs to act in your systems. An off-the-shelf service does what it does: the integrations in its catalogue, its own logic for handing over to a person, its own storage of conversations. If your CRM is custom-built and the data cannot be handed to a third-party service, the boxed product runs out of road quickly.

Custom development costs more at the start, but the agent lives inside your perimeter, works with your systems and obeys your rules: what data goes where, who sees the conversations, what the agent is allowed to do.

The sensible path is to start with a narrow scenario and look at the result. If a boxed product solves the task, you have your solution. If not, you already know which questions come in, where the agent goes wrong and what is missing — and development will start from a ready-made specification.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
body: Starting with the technology rather than the task. "We want AI" is not a task. "We answer 300 identical questions a week and can't keep up at weekends" is a task, and it comes with a ready way to measure the result.

Launching on everything at once. An agent that has to do everything — from support to accounting — does everything equally mediocrely. One narrow scenario brought up to standard is more useful than five half-finished ones.
Not preparing the knowledge base. An agent working from contradictory and outdated documents will give contradictory and outdated answers, and AI will get the blame.
Giving the agent unnecessary permissions. Write access where read access would have done, and actions without confirmation — that is how a single model error turns into an incident.

Not measuring. Without a set of test questions and metrics, a month later it is impossible to say whether the agent has got better or worse, and every argument about quality comes down to impressions.

sections.heading: Where to start
body: Pick one stream of enquiries that repeats most often and eats up time: support questions, sorting incoming enquiries, checking documents. Count how many such enquiries come in each week and how many minutes each one takes — that is your future saving and the project's main metric.

Gather the knowledge the agent will answer from: documents, answers to frequently asked questions, a hundred real enquiries with the correct answers. The agent will be tested against these enquiries both before launch and after.

Describe the boundaries: what the agent does by itself, what it only prepares for a person, and in which cases it must hand the conversation over. One page of such rules matters more than the choice of model.

And launch alongside people. For the first few weeks the agent works under your employees' supervision, the knowledge base is filled out from its misses, and it gets autonomy when the numbers back that up.

takeaways: What sets an agent apart from a chatbot or an assistant is that it acts in your systems: it finds an order, creates a deal, books a client. That is also why its mistakes cost more.
Agents do best at repetitive tasks whose answers are already in documents: first-line support, sorting incoming messages, working with documents, searching internal policies.

A model is confidently wrong when it doesn't know the answer. The cure is answering strictly from the documents found, narrow boundaries, verification of structured data and the right to say "I don't know".
The agent is given minimal permissions, a person confirms irreversible actions, and everything the agent does is logged.
Sending personal data to a foreign model is a cross-border transfer under 152-FZ. The alternative is a Russian provider or your own model on your own server.

One scenario — from {price:90000} and two weeks; several scenarios with CRM and knowledge base — from {price:180000}; end-to-end automation — from {price:350000}. Getting the data in order often takes longer than the development.

svoya-crm-ili-gotovaya.title: Custom CRM or off-the-shelf: when a ready-made system is enough and when it isn't
svoya-crm-ili-gotovaya.excerpt: How an off-the-shelf CRM differs from a custom one — not in features but in consequences: the ceilings boxed systems run into, the decisions you will have to make yourself, what development costs and why the right answer is most often not "or" but "and".
svoya-crm-ili-gotovaya.lead: The question "buy an off-the-shelf CRM or build your own" is almost never about features. Boxed systems have longer feature lists than any custom build, and on a comparison table the ready-made option always wins. The difference shows up later — when the company's process no longer fits into someone else's data model. Here we look at where that happens, what you will have to decide for yourself and what each path costs.
svoya-crm-ili-gotovaya.metaTitle: Custom vs off-the-shelf CRM: which to choose, what it costs
svoya-crm-ili-gotovaya.metaDescription: Off-the-shelf CRM vs custom development: where boxed systems hit a ceiling, what your own CRM costs and when a ready-made one with add-ons is enough.

sections.heading: "We need a CRM" is not yet a requirement
body: Different companies mean different things by the word CRM. For a sales team it is a deal pipeline and call reminders. For an agency, it is tracking projects, hours and invoices. For a service company, it is requests, field staff and a spare parts warehouse. For a manufacturer, it is orders, shipments and a link to the equipment. All four go by the same word, and that is the first reason the "custom or off-the-shelf" comparison goes wrong: people compare not systems but ideas of what a system should do.

So the conversation should start not with choosing a product but with one question: which process do you want to stop keeping in your head and in chat threads? An answer like "we are losing enquiries" points to a pipeline and reminders — exactly what off-the-shelf systems do well. An answer like "we don't know how much we make on a project, because some of the work is billed in dollars, some in roubles, and we pay contractors after the fact" points to accounting that a boxed system doesn't offer in the form you need.

The good news is that the first type of request doesn't need — and shouldn't get — a development project. The bad news is that an off-the-shelf system answers the second type only up to a certain scale, and the boundary is not visible straight away.

sections.heading: What an off-the-shelf system really gives you
body: An off-the-shelf CRM wins where it is usually underestimated: not in its features but in everything around them.

It works today. Not in four weeks, not in three months — tonight, after you sign up and import your contacts from a spreadsheet. For a company that is losing enquiries right now, that outweighs almost any argument about architecture.

It has a mobile app that somebody maintains. Your own app is a separate project with a separate budget, two app stores, update reviews and a release cycle. It is usually left out of the CRM development estimate, and then it turns out that the sales managers need to work from their phones.

It has ready-made integrations with telephony, email, messengers, accounting and cash registers. In your own system each of them is several days of work, plus a further number of days before it stops breaking.

And there are people for it on the job market. A specialist in setting up a widely used CRM can be hired within a week. Someone who knows their way around your own system cannot be hired at all — you can only grow one or keep paying the people who wrote it.
That is a serious list. It is worth giving up only when you get something in return that a boxed system fundamentally does not have.

sections.heading: Three ceilings companies run into
body: The first is the data model. An off-the-shelf system is built around the entities "lead", "contact", "company" and "deal". As long as your process maps onto them, all is well. As soon as an entity appears that this model doesn't have, people start imitating it with whatever is at hand: a project becomes a deal with extra fields, a production stage becomes a pipeline stage, a contractor becomes a contact with a tag. Each such substitution works, but adds a rule that exists only in the team's heads. A year later there are a couple of dozen such rules, and a new employee cannot understand why one deal means a sale and another means an installation stage.

The second is reporting. Reports in off-the-shelf systems are built on the fields the system considers important. When half the meaning lives in custom fields and unwritten agreements, the report starts to lie — not because it calculates incorrectly, but because it calculates the wrong thing. The typical outcome: the data is exported to Excel and counted by hand, which takes you right back to where you started.
The third is the total cost of ownership over several years. More on that separately below, because it is almost always calculated wrongly.
Importantly, none of these ceilings is hit in the first month. All three are a consequence of growth, and that is exactly why "start with an off-the-shelf system" is almost never a mistake.

sections.heading: What "your own CRM" really means
body: Your own system is not "the same thing, just with our fields". It means taking on decisions that, in an off-the-shelf system, someone has already made for you — decisions you didn't know existed, because they are not visible from the interface.

We don't know this from articles: we have our own CRM, which we wrote for ourselves and in which we keep leads, clients, projects, tasks and access credentials. Below are five decisions from it. They look like technical trivia, but each one stands behind a specific mistake that otherwise happens without fail.

sections.heading: Money: why amounts are stored in minor units
body: Money must not be stored as a fractional number. A computer cannot represent 0.1 and 0.2 exactly — their sum is not 0.3 but differs from it by a vanishingly small amount. On a single operation you won't notice. Across a few thousand rows the report starts to diverge from reality, first by small change, then by noticeable sums, and nobody can work out where the difference came from.

That is why our system stores every amount as an integer in the currency's smallest unit — kopecks or cents — and whole units appear only on screen and at the moment of entry. The field is called not "amount" but "amount in minor units", on purpose: if the field had silently changed its meaning, every place where someone forgot to update it would show a value a hundred times too large.
In an off-the-shelf CRM you don't need to think about this — it has already been done. In your own, you need to think about it before the first thousand rows appear in the database, not after.

sections.heading: Two currencies you must not add together
body: We bill some of our work in roubles and some in dollars. The obvious solution is to convert everything into one currency and show a grand total. We deliberately don't.

To add roubles to dollars you need an exchange rate. The rate changes. That means the total the report showed yesterday will be different tomorrow — even though not a single deal has changed. A total that changes on its own cannot be reconciled with anything, and trust in it disappears after the first mismatch with the accounts department.

So totals are calculated separately for each currency: two lines instead of one. It is slightly less convenient and completely honest. If a company really needs a single total, then it also needs an exchange rate fixed on the date of each transaction — and that is no longer a field but a separate mechanism, and it has to be designed deliberately.

sections.heading: Passwords: why the server must not see them
body: Access credentials inevitably end up in a CRM: hosting, domains, admin panels of client sites, email. The temptation is to keep them in an ordinary field like everything else. The problem is that the database leaves the server every night as a backup, and every such dump is a ready-made list of all the company's passwords.

Our passwords are encrypted right in the browser, with a key derived from a master passphrase that is never sent to the server. The server stores unreadable text and cannot decrypt it, even in theory. A backup is then worth exactly as much as a random string of characters.

This decision has a price, and you need to know it in advance: nobody can recover a forgotten master passphrase, including the owner of the server. Searching and checking passwords on the server side is also impossible — that would require the key, and with the key on the server the whole point is lost. This is not a shortcoming; it is the terms of the deal.

Off-the-shelf systems usually offer a credential store where decryption happens on their side. That is more convenient and protects against a different threat model. Choosing between the two approaches means choosing what exactly you are protecting yourself from, and that choice, too, is yours to make.

sections.heading: Deletion that doesn't delete straight away
body: The "delete" button in a record-keeping system should almost never delete immediately. People make mistakes, and a project deleted by accident along with its correspondence is a loss that nothing can make up for.

The standard solution is soft deletion: the record is marked as deleted and disappears from the lists. It has a side effect people forget about: if nothing ever deletes such records for real, they pile up forever and end up in every nightly backup. For client contacts, this directly contradicts Federal Law 152-FZ, Russia's personal data law, which expects personal data to be deleted once the purpose of processing it has been served.

So for us, deletion is a thirty-day grace period, not a graveyard: for a month the record can be restored from the trash, after which a daily job erases it for good. Notes are deleted together with the record, not before — otherwise a restored project would come back without its discussion, which is almost as bad as not coming back at all.

sections.heading: Statuses don't remind anyone of anything
body: The most common reason a deal is lost is not the lack of a CRM but a card quietly sitting in the status "in correspondence" for the fourth month running. A status cannot remind anyone of itself: it describes a state, not a commitment.

That is why the main field on our leads is not the status but the next step: a date and one line saying exactly what needs to be done. An overdue next step is the only thing that puts a lead on the main screen and into the morning digest. The line of description matters as much as the date: the reminder "call about the estimate — 3 days overdue" is clear without opening the card, while a bare "lead overdue" forces you to open it and try to remember.

The digest arrives in the team chat in the morning — and doesn't arrive at all if there is nothing to remind anyone of. A daily "all clear" teaches people not to open the bot, and then one day they scroll past something important.
Almost every off-the-shelf system has a reminder mechanism. The question is whether it is mandatory: if the "next step" field can be left empty, it will be left empty.

sections.heading: What a custom CRM costs
body: With us, CRM development starts at {price:400000} and four weeks — that is a system on a ready-made architecture with the core modules, roles, basic integrations and data migration. Processes built to fit, dashboards, integrations with services and telephony, and team training start at {price:700000} and eight weeks. A complex platform with access rights split by department and designed for high load starts at {price:1200000} and twelve weeks.

To this you have to honestly add what usually doesn't make it into the development estimate. Changes after launch — in the first months the system changes constantly, because real work always differs from what was described at the start. Hosting and backups. Dependency and security updates. And the most expensive item — the availability of people who can make changes.
It is worth budgeting around 15–20% of the development cost per year for support. Less than that means the system will age and one day need not changes but a rewrite.

sections.heading: What an off-the-shelf system costs over three years
body: The cost of an off-the-shelf system is almost always calculated from the licence price, and that is almost always wrong. You need to add up four things.

The subscription — usually per user per month, and it grows with the team. Implementation — setting up pipelines, permissions and templates and importing data; that is separate work done by an integrator. Customisation — everything that can't be set up with checkboxes and needs modules or scripts; over time this is the least predictable line item. And migration — the cost of leaving if you ever decide to go.

The last item is the one people notice last. Data in an off-the-shelf system can be exported, but it is exported in that system's model: deals with stages, fields with internal names, files as a separate archive. The links between entities and the process logic aren't exported at all, because they live in the settings. The longer and more deeply you are in the system, the more it costs to leave.

Over a one-year horizon, off-the-shelf is almost always cheaper. Over three to five years, for a team that actively customises the system, the gap narrows and sometimes flips. There is no universal answer here — there is arithmetic worth doing with your own numbers.

sections.heading: The hybrid that is most often what you need
body: The "custom or off-the-shelf" opposition is false more often than it seems. The option that works is usually in the middle: the off-the-shelf CRM stays where it is strong — the pipeline, calls, correspondence, the mobile app — and alongside it you add your own services for whatever doesn't fit its model.

A client or partner portal with your own calculation logic. Production or field work tracking. A dashboard for a department that needs something other than what the CRM shows. Pricing by your own formula. All of this lives separately and exchanges data with the CRM through an integration.

This approach has a price — synchronisation. Two systems sharing data will inevitably drift apart unless you decide in advance which one is the master for each entity. The rule is simple and non-negotiable: every entity has exactly one owner, and the others read. A client is created in the CRM and the portal reads it; an order is created in the portal and the CRM reads it. As soon as both sides start writing to the same field, manual reconciliation begins.
In return, there is less development, the ceiling goes away, and you don't have to move anywhere.

sections.heading: How to choose: a short checklist
body: Off-the-shelf is enough if your process is enquiries, calls and deals; if the team is up to 15–20 people; if you need to start within the next few weeks; if you are not prepared to fund development on an ongoing basis.

A custom system is worth considering if the key entity of your business isn't called a "deal" and can't be represented as one without stretching; if half your data lives in custom fields and unwritten agreements; if reports are calculated in Excel anyway; if data cannot leave your infrastructure because of client or regulatory requirements; if you are already paying an integrator so much that the three-year total is comparable to development.
And separately: if you can't describe your process on one page, neither system will help. Automating an undescribed process gives you an undescribed process that now also has a database.

sections.heading: When you don't need a custom CRM
body: You don't need one if the main problem is discipline, not the tool. A system won't make anyone call; it will only show that nobody did.

You don't need one if the process changes every month. Development fixes the process in code, and fixing something that hasn't settled yet means rewriting it. At this stage an off-the-shelf system, or even a spreadsheet, is more useful.

You don't need one if nobody is going to be responsible for it. A system needs an owner inside the company — not a developer, but someone who decides how things should be. Without one, any CRM, custom or off-the-shelf, turns into a dumping ground of cards within six months.

And you don't need one if you haven't tried an off-the-shelf system yet. A month of working in a boxed product gives you a list of specific complaints, and that is the best specification you can bring to a developer. Without it, development starts with guesswork.

sections.heading: Where to start
body: Describe the one process that hurts most on a single page: who does what, in what order and what counts as the result. See whether it maps onto the entities of an off-the-shelf system without stretching. If it does, take the off-the-shelf one and come back to this question in a year. If it doesn't, you already know exactly what needs to be developed, and the conversation with a contractor won't start from scratch.

We do both: we design custom CRMs and platforms, and we connect the missing services to existing systems. If you're not sure which path is yours, write to us — we'll go through your process and tell you honestly if an off-the-shelf system will do.

takeaways: The "custom or off-the-shelf" question is decided not by a feature list but by whether the core entity of your business maps onto the "lead — contact — deal" model without stretching.
An off-the-shelf system wins on what surrounds the features: it works today, and it comes with a mobile app, ready-made integrations and specialists on the job market.

A custom CRM means the decisions a boxed system has already made for you: storing money in minor units, never adding different currencies together, encrypting passwords in the browser, deferred deletion, a mandatory next step.

Development starts at {price:400000} and four weeks, plus 15–20% of the cost per year for support; the cost of an off-the-shelf system must include the subscription, implementation, customisation and the price of leaving.
Most often the right answer is a hybrid: an off-the-shelf CRM for the pipeline plus your own services for whatever doesn't fit into it, with one owner for every entity.
If the process isn't described on one page or nobody is responsible for the system, development won't help — start with an off-the-shelf system and come back to the question in a year.

skolko-stoit-sajt.title: How much does a website cost in 2026: what goes into the price
skolko-stoit-sajt.excerpt: Real prices for a business-card site, landing page, corporate website, B2B site and online store: what makes up the estimate, what drives the cost up, what is usually not included, and how to compare contractors' proposals.
skolko-stoit-sajt.lead: Website development prices can differ tenfold or more, and that is not always greed on one side and price dumping on the other: the word "website" covers very different products. Let's go through them by type — business-card site, landing page, corporate website, B2B and online store — and look at what each costs, what goes into the price, what it usually leaves out, and how to read an estimate so that you neither overpay nor cut costs in a way that hurts you.
skolko-stoit-sajt.metaTitle: How much does a website cost in 2026: prices explained
skolko-stoit-sajt.metaDescription: Website prices in 2026: business-card site, landing page, corporate, B2B and online store. What makes up the estimate, what raises it and what support costs.

sections.heading: Why one question gets answers from {price:20000} to {price:1000000}
body: Ask five contractors how much a website costs and you will get five answers that differ tenfold. That does not necessarily mean someone is cheating: the word "website" covers half a dozen different products, and comparing their prices is like comparing the price of a bicycle and a lorry because both count as "transport".

A one-page business-card site with contact details and a twenty-page corporate website integrated with a CRM differ in workload not by a few percent but several times over. An online store adds a catalogue, a basket, payment and delivery — and each of these components is a project in its own right. A site for B2B sales brings price lists, calculators, partner accounts and data exchange with 1C (the accounting system most Russian companies run on) along with it.

So the honest answer to "how much does it cost" starts with a question back: what kind of site, and what for. Below is a breakdown by type with real prices, what makes them up, what they usually leave out, and how to compare proposals so that you neither overpay nor cut costs in a way that hurts you.

sections.heading: What makes up the price
body: A website is not a product off the shelf but the work of several specialists, and the price consists almost entirely of their hours. Someone designs the structure and the visitor's journey, someone draws the design, someone codes the layout and programs, someone writes the copy, sets up integrations, tests on different devices and launches.

Each of these stages can be done quickly using ready-made solutions, or slowly and tailored to you. The design can be an existing template adapted to your brand identity — or a unique layout built from scratch. You can send your own copy, or order copy with the structure worked out. A request form can send an email to your inbox — or create a deal in the CRM with its source and the ad campaign tag.

Hence the main rule for reading any price: it depends not on "beauty" but on the number of decisions that have to be made for your particular task. The more that is standard, the cheaper and faster. The more that is special — logic, integrations, content — the more expensive, and that is not a mark-up but honest time.
All the figures below are the lower bound, "from". The final amount is fixed after the brief, once the scope is clear: how many pages, whose copy, which systems to connect to.

sections.heading: Business-card website: from {price:29000}
body: A business-card site is a single page that answers three questions: who you are, what you do and how to reach you. Services, advantages, contacts, a map, a request form. That is enough for a tradesperson, a small studio, a consultant, or a company that simply needs to be present online and not look suspicious when someone checks it out.

Our basic business-card site on a ready-made solution adapted to your brand costs from {price:29000} and takes from five days. A version with custom design, messenger contact buttons, basic SEO and analytics starts at {price:49000}. A unique design with animations, copywriting and integrations starts at {price:90000}.

The main limitation of a business-card site is that it is one page. It is almost impossible to attract search traffic for different services with it: a search engine needs a separate page for each query. If search promotion is in your plans, that is an argument for looking at a multi-page site straight away — or at least building the business-card site so that it can be expanded later without starting over.

sections.heading: Landing page: from {price:59000}
body: A landing page is also a single page, but its job is different: not to tell people about the company but to sell one specific offer to someone who arrived from an ad. Hence a different structure — offer, benefits, objections, proof, call to action — and different requirements for speed and analytics.

A basic landing page on a ready-made solution, with up to six content screens, a form and analytics connected, starts at {price:59000} and takes from 7–10 days. With custom design built around the offer, a quiz or request calculator, CRM integration and goals configured for advertising — from {price:98000}. A unique design, A/B versions for different traffic sources, a worked-out structure and copywriting — from {price:180000}.

A landing page shows especially clearly why integrations and goals cost money. Advertising without proper analytics is a budget of which you cannot say which part actually worked. A quiz instead of a five-field form usually brings in more leads, but only if its results reach a sales manager rather than sitting in someone's inbox.

sections.heading: Corporate and end-to-end websites: from {price:89000} to {price:400000}
body: A multi-page site is the main format for a company that wants to win clients from search and look solid to people who come on a recommendation. Separate pages for services, the company, case studies, contacts, sometimes a blog — each with its own job and its own search query.

An end-to-end website on a ready-made template with content for up to eight pages costs from {price:89000}. With custom design, copywriting, CRM integration and an SEO foundation — from {price:150000}. Bespoke development with complex scenarios — from {price:280000}.

A corporate website is the same category, but with an emphasis on the brand and a larger structure. The basic version, up to seven pages with content, starts at {price:120000} and takes from ten days. Custom design for your brand, up to fifteen pages with copywriting, integration with a CRM and messengers, extended SEO and analytics — from {price:220000} and from three weeks. Unique design, complex structure and functionality, support after launch — from {price:400000} and from five weeks.

The biggest variable here is the number of pages and who writes the copy for them. A service page with a well-thought-out structure, answers to questions and examples takes a copywriter half a day to a day each, and with fifteen pages this line of the estimate easily becomes the largest.

sections.heading: B2B website: from {price:180000}
body: A B2B site sells not to a person but to a company, and nobody buys on it in one click. The visitor is a procurement specialist, an engineer or a manager who needs to quickly find specifications, download a price list, estimate the cost and request a quote — and then the decision is made by four people in a meeting.

The basic version on a ready-made solution, with a catalogue, price lists, a quote request form and basic integrations, starts at {price:180000} and takes from three weeks. With custom design, a cost calculator, a partner account and CRM integration — from {price:320000}. Complex deal logic, data exchange with 1C and internal systems, a dealer portal — from {price:550000} and from eight weeks.

A B2B site almost always gets more expensive because of accounting systems. Prices and stock levels that live in 1C have to be shown on the site up to date, otherwise managers will spend every day explaining to clients why "the website shows a different price". Setting up that exchange reliably is a separate and not particularly quick piece of work.

sections.heading: Online store: from {price:190000}
body: A store is the "heaviest" type of website, because it does not just tell — it sells on its own: catalogue, filters, product pages, basket, checkout, payment, delivery, notifications, customer account. Each of these components has to work without human involvement, including at night and at weekends.

A basic store on a ready-made solution with a catalogue of up to a hundred products, a basket, online payment and delivery set up starts at {price:190000} and takes from three weeks. With custom design and filters, a customer account and integration with 1C and a CRM — from {price:350000}. A large catalogue, marketplace scenarios, complex inventory accounting and content loading — from {price:600000} and from eight weeks.

It is also worth remembering that accepting payments in Russia means an online cash register and receipts under 54-FZ (the federal law on cash registers), and collecting names, phone numbers and addresses brings the obligations of a personal data operator. These are not development costs, but they are part of the launch, and it is better to learn about them before it.

And a word on content. A hundred product pages with photos, descriptions and specifications is a volume of work that is underestimated more often than anything else. If you have hundreds of products, they should be exported from your accounting system rather than typed in by hand.

sections.heading: Ready-made solution or development from scratch
body: In almost every category the basic version is built on a ready-made solution — a proven foundation that is adapted to your brand. This is not "a dirt-cheap template off the internet" but a way of not paying to reinvent what was invented long ago: menus, forms, responsive layout, loading speed.

This route is faster and cheaper and works perfectly well when the task is standard: tell people about your services, collect leads, show a catalogue. There is only one limitation — anything non-standard has to be fitted into someone else's logic, and at some point that becomes more expensive than building your own.

Custom development is justified when the website is part of a business process rather than a shop window. A complex calculator, a personal account with data from your systems, special ordering logic, a load that ready-made solutions are not designed for. Then you are paying for a site that works exactly the way your business is organised, not the other way round.
A sensible strategy for many is to start with a ready-made foundation, check that the site brings in clients, and only then invest in custom work where you have hit the ceiling.

sections.heading: What drives the cost up
body: Copy. The most underestimated item. A page that sells needs structure, facts and answers to objections — that is work, not "throwing together a couple of paragraphs". If you have no copy of your own, its cost needs to be budgeted from the start, otherwise the launch will stall on empty pages.

Integrations with undocumented systems. Connecting a site to a popular CRM is a well-understood task. Connecting it to an in-house accounting system that nobody remembers how it works is research first and development second.

Moving from an old site. If your current site ranks in search, those rankings need to be preserved: migrate the content, set up redirects from the old URLs to the new ones, check that nothing has been lost. Without this, a beautiful new site brings in less than the ugly old one for its first few months.
Multiple languages, non-standard animation, complex user roles, heightened security requirements — each of these adds scope, sometimes significantly.

And approvals. A project where the mock-up is signed off by five people with different opinions takes longer and costs more than one with a single person in charge. This is not about the client's personality but about the fact that every iteration is hours.

sections.heading: What is usually not included in the price
body: Domain and hosting. They are registered in the client's name and paid for separately — and rightly so: the site's address should belong to you, not the contractor. For a small site that means a few dollars a year for the domain and a few dollars a month for hosting.

Paid licences and services: commercial CMSs and modules, an online cash register, SMS notifications, paid maps, mailing services. Their cost depends on the solutions chosen and the volume, and goes on a separate line.

Photos and video. If you have none of your own, a photo shoot or bought images are budgeted separately. Stock photos of "smiling partners" are worse than honest phone photos from your own production floor.

Advertising and promotion. The SEO foundation in the estimate is the right technical base: structure, meta tags, speed, markup. That is not the same as promotion — ongoing work on content and search queries that happens after launch and is paid for separately.

sections.heading: What a website costs after launch
body: Launch is not the end of the spending. The minimum is the domain and hosting, which is pocket change. Beyond that, everything depends on how alive the site is: whether prices change, whether new services come out, whether advertising drives traffic to it.

If the site is static and changes once every six months, ongoing support is unnecessary — one-off edits as needed will do. If it is a store, a B2B portal or a site with integrations, it needs looking after: updating the engine and modules, checking that form submissions arrive, that the exchange with 1C has not stalled, that backups are being made.

Support with monitoring, backups, minor edits and a pool of hours for tasks costs from {price:40000/mo} with us; with priority and feature development — from {price:80000/mo}; a dedicated team with SLA guarantees — from {price:150000/mo}. A one-off format with no subscription fee is also possible.

A separate word on security. A site that has not been updated for years is the most common entry point for a hack: outdated modules with publicly known vulnerabilities are hunted for automatically and at scale. Updates are not a contractor's whim but insurance.

sections.heading: How to compare proposals
body: Compare what is included, not the total. A {price:80000} proposal and a {price:200000} proposal often describe different websites. Ask for the estimate to be broken down by stage and look at what it contains: how many pages, whose design, who writes the copy, which integrations, how many rounds of revisions.

Ask who will own the site. The code, hosting access, the admin panel, the domain — all of it should be registered to you. A site on a contractor's closed platform that cannot be taken away turns a change of contractor into a new development project.
Clarify what counts as launch and what happens afterwards. Is there a warranty period during which bugs are fixed free of charge? Who makes changes three months later, and for how much?
And pay attention to the questions they ask you. A contractor who names a price without asking where your clients will come from and what they should do on the site is selling hours, not results.

sections.heading: Why a cheap website can end up costing more
body: A cheap site is a perfectly fine choice if you need to test an idea quickly or simply get online. Problems start when it is bought as a permanent solution, which it is not.

A typical scenario: a {price:20000} site that is not responsive and loads slowly. Advertising it gets more expensive, because visitors on phones leave before it has loaded. A year later it is rebuilt — and you pay a second time, the full price now, and lose time on top.
Another scenario is a site built on the contractor's own website builder that cannot be moved. It works as long as you keep paying, and when you change contractor it has to be rebuilt from scratch.

The sensible place to save is not the quality of the foundation but the scope: launch fewer pages, but well made, and expand as the site starts bringing in clients. A business-card site built with the future in mind is later developed into a full website rather than thrown away.

sections.heading: How to save without losing out
body: Prepare materials in advance. Copy, photos, logo, company details, a list of services with prices — everything expected from you is best gathered before the start. A project standing idle while it waits for content costs both sides money.
Appoint one person in charge. Someone who collects feedback from everyone and makes the decisions saves weeks of approvals.

Start with what matters most. Decide which pages and features are needed for the first leads and which can wait. Integration with 1C, a customer account and a blog are often best left for a second phase, once it is clear that the site works.

And do not skimp on analytics. Goals, counters and reliable hand-off of leads are an inexpensive part of the estimate, and without them it is impossible to tell whether the site has paid for itself at all.

takeaways: "Website" means six different products: a business-card site from {price:29000}, a landing page from {price:59000}, an end-to-end website from {price:89000}, a corporate site from {price:120000}, B2B from {price:180000}, an online store from {price:190000}.
The price consists almost entirely of specialists' hours and grows with the number of decisions made for your task: design, copy, integrations.
The main cost drivers are copy, integrations with undocumented systems, moving from an old site while keeping its search rankings, and lengthy approvals.
Domain, hosting, paid licences, photo shoots and promotion usually come separately; the domain and hosting should be registered in the client's name.
Compare proposals by the scope of work and by who will own the code and access, not by the total.
Save on scope, not on the quality of the foundation: fewer pages at launch, but built to grow.

telegram-bot-dlya-biznesa.title: Telegram bots for business: what they automate and what they cost
telegram-bot-dlya-biznesa.excerpt: Which jobs a bot really takes on, how a Mini App differs from an ordinary bot, where CRM and payment integrations break, what development and upkeep cost — and when a business does not need a bot at all.
telegram-bot-dlya-biznesa.lead: A Telegram bot looks like a cheap substitute for a website and an app: describe the scenario, get the enquiries. In practice half of all bots go quiet within a month — usually not because they were badly built, but because they were given a job the company does not have. Here is what bots are genuinely given to do, how they differ from a Mini App, what they cost and when you are better off not building one.
telegram-bot-dlya-biznesa.metaTitle: Telegram bots for business: uses, timelines, prices
telegram-bot-dlya-biznesa.metaDescription: What a Telegram bot automates, how a Mini App differs from a bot, where CRM and payment integrations break, and what development and upkeep cost.

sections.heading: What a bot is, from a business point of view
body: A Telegram bot is a program that works inside a chat: it receives messages and button presses, replies according to set logic and talks to other systems — your CRM, a spreadsheet, a payment service, your database. There is no artificial intelligence in it by default: a bot does exactly what is built into its scenario.

Its main advantage is that it lives where people already are. No app to install, no password to invent, no confirmation email to wait for. Follow a link, press one "Start" button — and the conversation has begun. For tasks where every extra step kills half the enquiries, that is the decisive difference from a website, and even more so from a mobile app.

The second property is less obvious, but it shapes the whole mechanism: a bot can message a person first only after that person has contacted it. You cannot buy a subscriber base, upload one from a file or assemble one from your clients' phone numbers. The bot earns every contact itself — and that same rule keeps it from turning into a spam channel.

Hence a simple rule: a bot is good wherever there is a repeated action — booking, checking a status, leaving an enquiry, reporting in. And it is poor where one complex choice needs discussion: that will end in a conversation with a person anyway, and it is better if the bot gets the person there in three touches rather than thirty.

sections.heading: Five jobs most often handed to a bot
body: Taking enquiries. The bot asks three or four questions, collects contact details and passes the enquiry to a manager or straight into the CRM. The value is not in the form itself — the website has one too — but in the fact that the person does not leave the messenger and answers the questions one at a time instead of staring at a ten-field questionnaire.

Bookings and reminders. Beauty salons, clinics, car repair shops, tutors — anything with a schedule. The bot shows free slots, records the booking and sends a reminder a day ahead. The reminder is where the real economics lie: it cuts no-shows, and every no-show is an empty slot in the schedule that you have already paid for in rent and wages.

Order statuses and notifications. "Where is my order?" is the most common support question in almost any business that delivers. If the status arrives on its own, the question simply never comes up, and first-line support stops reading the spreadsheet back to people.

Answers to routine questions. Opening hours, address, delivery terms, warranty, documents. Here the bot replaces not a person but the tenth repetition of the same answer. The same layer usually handles free-form questions too — when a question does not match a button, but the answer to it is in your knowledge base.

Internal processes. The most underrated part: staff requests to IT or facilities, approvals, reports from sites, collecting photos from installation jobs. A bot like this has no marketing and no leads — but it does away with correspondence spread across ten chats and "I sent it to you, scroll up".

sections.heading: Bot or Mini App: what is the difference
body: An ordinary bot communicates through messages, buttons and commands. A Mini App is a full interface inside Telegram: screens, lists, filters, forms, a basket, payment. Technically it is a web application that opens right inside the messenger, with no browser and nothing to install.

The choice is simple. If the scenario is linear and fits into five to ten steps, a bot will do the job better: it is faster, lighter and needs no design. If you need a catalogue with pictures, filters, a personal account, order history — that is Mini App territory, because flicking through a hundred products with buttons is impossible.

Most often the two are combined: the bot acts as the entry point and the notification channel, and the Mini App as the shopfront and the account. The user taps a button in the chat, opens a screen, places an order and gets notifications back in the conversation.

It is important to remember that a Mini App is a web application, with everything that implies. It has to be hosted somewhere, load quickly on a phone and behave properly on a poor connection. The requirements are the same as for the mobile version of a website, and the amount of work is to match.

sections.heading: How a bot works under the hood
body: All communication goes through the Bot API. A bot is created in @BotFather, which issues a token — in effect the bot's password. Whoever holds the token is the bot: they can read incoming messages and write on its behalf. That is why the token is kept in the server's secrets, not in the code, let alone in the repository.

A bot receives messages in one of two ways. Long polling: the program itself periodically asks Telegram whether there is anything new; it works anywhere, including on a local machine without a domain. Webhook: Telegram knocks on your address itself; you need a domain with valid HTTPS, but there is no constant polling. For most tasks the difference is unnoticeable, but for debugging the first method is far more convenient.

The key consequence: a bot needs a server running around the clock. A bot is not a file "uploaded to hosting" but a process that has to be alive at three in the morning, when a client decides to check their order status.

The state of the conversation has to be stored somewhere too. If the bot remembers the scenario step only in memory, any restart — and one happens with every update — drops half the users in the middle of a questionnaire. A proper implementation keeps state in a database, and from the user's point of view the restart goes unnoticed.

And a word about limits. Telegram caps the sending rate — around thirty messages per second in general, and noticeably stricter for groups. A broadcast to tens of thousands of people does not go out instantly; it has to be spread out through a queue. Trying to fire it all at once ends in errors and temporary restrictions on the bot.

sections.heading: Integrations: where things usually break
body: The most common integration is the CRM. An enquiry from the bot should become a deal with its source recorded, not a message in a shared chat that someone will notice one day. Without that, the bot turns into yet another channel nobody looks through.

Next in popularity come spreadsheets. Google Sheets is great for testing a hypothesis in a day and seeing the first enquiries. As permanent storage it is poor: no access rights, no history, and anyone can sort a column and shift the data out of line with the rest.

Payments, calendars, inventory, 1C (the accounting system most Russian companies run on), delivery services — all of these connect through APIs, and this is where the real work begins. Someone else's service lives its own life: it changes its response format, revokes keys, goes down for maintenance.

An integration usually breaks not at launch, when everything is being checked, but after several months of quiet. That is why, in a production bot, every external call has a retry on failure and an alert to the person responsible. The worst case is not an error but silence: enquiries stopped reaching the CRM, and you found out two weeks later from your revenue.

It is also worth agreeing on what the source of truth is. If the bot writes to the CRM while a manager edits the same deal by hand, you need to decide in advance whose data wins when they diverge. This conversation seems tedious right up until the first conflict.

sections.heading: Payments inside Telegram
body: There are two ways to take money. The first is Telegram's built-in payments through a connected provider: the person never leaves the messenger, and payment happens in the same window. The second is a link to an ordinary payment page; it looks less smooth, but it is quicker to set up and does not depend on the list of supported providers.

Digital goods and subscriptions inside Telegram follow separate mechanics — payment in Stars. The platform's rules on this change from time to time, so the specific method is worth confirming at the start of the project rather than building it in blind.

Whatever you choose, in Russia accepting payment means an online cash register and a receipt under 54-FZ, the Russian law on fiscal receipts. Fiscalisation is usually handled by the payment provider, but you need to check that before launch, not after the first sale: the receipt is the seller's obligation, not the bot developer's.

And think refunds through in advance. In a bot this is not a button but a process: who makes the decision, within what time frame, how the money is returned and what the client sees along the way. Silence in response to a refund request costs more than the amount itself — it ends up in the reviews.

sections.heading: Personal data and 152-FZ
body: As soon as a bot asks for a name, phone number, address or date of birth, it is collecting personal data — with all the obligations of a data operator under Federal Law 152-FZ, Russia's personal data law. You need consent, you need an accessible processing policy, and the data is supposed to be stored in a database located in Russia.

The practical approach is to collect less. Every extra field in a questionnaire is not only a minus for conversion but a plus for liability. If a name and phone number are enough for a booking, a bot never needs passport details.

A separate point about the conversations themselves. Everything a person sends the bot physically passes through your server and is often saved there in logs. Photos of documents, card numbers sent "just in case", medical details — all of it settles in text files nobody remembers. Logs should be cleaned on a schedule, and full message contents should not be written to them.

sections.heading: What development costs
body: The price is made up of four things: how many scenarios, how many integrations, whether there is a custom interface and what load is expected. A bot that takes an enquiry and puts it into the CRM and a bot with a personal account, payments and inventory are different projects, several times apart in cost, even though both go by the same word.

Here is how it looks with us. A basic bot built to a ready scenario: from {price:50000} and from a week of work — menu, buttons, taking enquiries, notifications to a chat or the CRM, launch on your account. A package combining a Mini App, CRM and payments: from {price:110000} and from two weeks. A project with complex logic, custom integrations, analytics and headroom for load: from {price:220000} and from four weeks.

What usually drives the price up is not "lots of buttons" but integration with an in-house system that has no documentation: first you have to work out how it is built, and only then connect anything. Roles and permissions have a similar effect — when a bot has several types of users, each with their own set of actions.

It comes out cheaper when three things are ready before the start: a clear one-page scenario, access to the systems it needs to connect to, and a person on your side who answers questions within a day rather than a week.

sections.heading: What upkeep costs
body: A server for a bot is inexpensive — a simple bot needs only the smallest virtual machine, which costs just a few dollars a month. A Mini App with images and traffic will cost more, but even so it is not the main expense.

The main one is changes. A business changes its prices, services and rules, and the scenario has to follow. A bot nobody has touched for a year usually tells clients about last year's terms — and that is worse than having no bot at all.

There is a technical side too: Telegram evolves, the API changes, dependencies go out of date. Once every year or eighteen months the project needs a round of updates, even if nothing has changed functionally.

And one question to settle before launch: who fixes the bot if it goes silent on a Saturday? The answer "the developer will probably take a look" means downtime on your busiest day. The answer "support under contract, response within so many hours" means someone has thought it through.

sections.heading: Bot builder or custom development
body: Bot builders exist, they are cheap and for linear scenarios they work perfectly well: put together a questionnaire, hand out a lead magnet, walk a person through a five-step funnel. If that is your task, there is no point starting development from scratch.

Their limitations are just as clear. The only logic possible is what the platform provides; your clients' data sits with the service, not with you; the subscription fee grows along with your base; there is nowhere to plug in a non-standard integration. And the whole bot depends on whatever happens to someone else's business.

Development is needed when the bot is tied to your systems, when the logic does not fit into a builder, when owning the data and the code matters — or when the builder's bill for a large base is already comparable to the cost of development.

A sensible sequence usually goes like this: test demand on a builder, and when you hit its ceiling and it becomes clear exactly what you need, move the logic into a solution of your own. By then practice itself has written the requirements, and the project comes out cheaper than if everything had been designed up front.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
body: A maze with no exit. A bot with no way through to a human is more irritating than waiting on hold. The "Call a manager" button should be visible at every step, not hidden on the third level of the menu.

A bot instead of a process. If there is nobody to handle the enquiries, a bot will not help — it will just bring more people to the same bottleneck faster. It makes sense to automate what already works but takes a lot of hands.

Broadcasts as the only value. A subscriber who gets nothing but promotions from a bot unsubscribes within two weeks. A useful action — an order status, a reminder, an answer to a question — keeps the person in the conversation and makes an occasional broadcast welcome.

No analytics. Without events for each step of the scenario, there is no way to know where people drop off. Usually it is one specific question in the questionnaire that is worded unclearly, and it takes five minutes to find — if the data is being collected.
Launch and forget. A bot is a service, not a gift. It needs an owner on the business side, regular review of the conversations and a clear procedure for making changes to the scenario.

sections.heading: When you do not need a bot
body: When there are few enquiries. Two or three enquiries a week are cheaper to handle by hand — automation will never pay for itself here, yet it will still need maintaining.

When the deal is complex and one-off. Equipment costing upwards of {price:1000000}, project work, anything sold through discussion and negotiation — here a bot is useful at most as a quick way to set up a meeting.

When your audience is not on Telegram. If your clients message you on WhatsApp or phone you, a bot in a different messenger will not create a flow of enquiries by itself — it serves existing demand rather than generating new demand.
When there is no process. If inside the company it is unclear who handles an enquiry and by when, a bot will only lock that uncertainty in and make it public.

sections.heading: Where to start
body: Pick one action that is repeated most often and eats up your staff's time: booking, status, a routine question, taking an enquiry. Count how many times a week it happens and how many minutes it takes — that is your future saving, the baseline you can later measure the result against.

Describe the scenario in words, on one page: what the person writes, what the bot replies, where automation ends and the manager takes over. A document like this matters more than any technical specification — it shows straight away where the scenario falls apart.
Decide where the data goes and who is responsible for it. An enquiry with no recipient is a lost enquiry, however nicely the bot collected it.
And launch narrow. One working scenario that delivers value from the first week is more useful than twenty buttons, half of which nobody will ever reach. Expanding is always easier than fixing.

takeaways: A bot works where there is a repeated action: booking, order status, a routine question, taking an enquiry. For a complex one-off deal it is useless.
A bot can message a person first only after that person has started the conversation — a subscriber base cannot be bought or uploaded.
A bot is a round-the-clock process on a server, not a file on hosting: it needs somewhere to keep conversation state, monitoring and an owner.
Integrations break not at launch but months later. Without retries on failure and an alert to the person responsible, enquiries vanish silently.
Taking payments means an online cash register and a receipt under 54-FZ; collecting phone numbers brings the obligations of a personal data operator under 152-FZ.

A simple bot starts from {price:50000} and a week; a bundle with a Mini App, CRM and payments from {price:110000}. The most expensive part is integration with an in-house system that has no documentation.

audit-bezopasnosti-sajtov.title: Website security audit: what gets checked and how it works
audit-bezopasnosti-sajtov.excerpt: What exactly is examined when a website is checked for vulnerabilities, how an audit differs from a penetration test and a scanner, what turns up most often, and how to tell that you have already been hacked.
audit-bezopasnosti-sajtov.lead: A website hack rarely looks like it does in the films. More often it is a quiet leak of your customer database, spam sent from your domain, or someone else's crypto miner on your server, noticed only through the hosting bill. A security audit is a way to find the holes before someone else does. Below we look at what exactly gets checked and how the process works from the inside.
audit-bezopasnosti-sajtov.metaTitle: Website security audit: what is checked and how it works
audit-bezopasnosti-sajtov.metaDescription: What a website security audit is, how it differs from a pentest and a scan, the OWASP Top 10 checks, common findings and signs your site is already hacked.

sections.heading: What a security audit is
body: A security audit is a systematic check of a website and its environment for vulnerabilities: errors in the code, weak server settings, outdated dependencies, and careless handling of user data and access rights.

The key word is "systematic". The job is not to run a scanner and hand over its log, but to look at the system through an attacker's eyes: what can be obtained, where you can go from there, and what it will cost the owner. A vulnerability on its own is an abstraction; the value of an audit is that it translates it into clear consequences. "Access to the database backup is open" sounds technical; "anyone can download your entire customer database" is clear.
The result is not a list of warnings but a prioritised document: what needs fixing today, what can be scheduled for a sprint, and what simply needs to be noted.

sections.heading: Audit, penetration test and scanner: what's the difference
body: Three terms that are constantly confused, even though they cost different amounts and deliver different things.

Automated scanning: a program crawls the site and checks it against a database of known problems, such as an outdated CMS version, an open port, a missing header or a component with a publicly disclosed vulnerability. It is fast, cheap and often free. The limitation is fundamental: a scanner does not understand what your application means. It will never work out that a manager who puts someone else's ID into the URL can see another department's deal, because technically that is a valid request returning a valid response.

A security audit is scanning plus manual work: a specialist studies the logic, roles and scenarios and checks what a machine cannot. The goal is to find as many problems as possible and describe how to close them.

A penetration test (pentest) has a different goal: not to compile a complete list, but to show that the defences can be breached at all. A pentester looks for a way in, and having found one, often doesn't spend time on the rest. It is proof of a vulnerability, not a map of every hole.

For a site that has never been checked before, an audit is usually what you need: it gives the full picture. A pentest makes more sense once basic hygiene is in place and you need to put the defences to a real test.

sections.heading: When to get checked
body: Before launch. It is cheaper to find a problem before the site has real users and their data.
After a major update. A new customer account area, online payments, an integration with an external service: each such feature adds entry points that weren't there before.
When you change contractors. You are taking over someone else's code and don't know what is in it. It is also a good reason to check who still has access to the server and the admin panel.
When a partner or client requires it. In tenders and corporate contracts, a security check increasingly appears as a separate item.
After an incident. Here the audit answers not only "what is vulnerable" but also "how did they get in, and are they still inside".

And regularly, if the site has customer accounts, payments or personal data. Code changes, dependencies age and new vulnerabilities are published every week, so a one-off check reflects only the day it was carried out.

sections.heading: What gets checked: the OWASP Top 10
body: The check is built on the OWASP Top 10, the widely accepted list of the most common and dangerous classes of web vulnerabilities. It is updated every few years and serves as a common language: if a contractor says "we checked against OWASP", it is clear what they mean.

Broken access control. The most common and most underestimated category: a user gets something they are not entitled to. The classic examples are substituting someone else's ID in a URL or a request, reaching admin sections via a direct link, and changing other people's records.
Cryptographic failures. Passwords stored without proper hashing, data sent over HTTP, home-made "encryption", tokens that cannot be revoked.
Injection. Someone else's code slipped in through input fields and request parameters: SQL, operating system commands, cross-site scripting (XSS). A classic of the genre that has not gone anywhere.

Insecure design. The problem lies not in a specific line of code but in the concept: password recovery via the question "mother's maiden name", no limit on the number of attempts, trusting data that came from the client.
Security misconfiguration. Debug mode on the production server, default accounts, unnecessary open ports, detailed error messages with stack traces, accessible service directories.
Outdated components. CMSs, plugins and libraries with publicly disclosed vulnerabilities. The most mechanical category, and at the same time the most widespread.
Authentication failures. Weak password requirements, sessions that never expire, no second factor where one is needed, improper logout.
Data and update integrity. Installing packages and updates from unverified sources, no signatures.
Insufficient logging. If nobody saw the attack, it carries on. Without logs, after an incident you will not be able to work out either how they got in or what they managed to take.
Server-side request forgery (SSRF). At the user's instruction, the application sends requests to internal addresses that should not be reachable from outside.

sections.heading: What gets checked besides the code
body: An application vulnerability is only part of the picture. Just as many problems are found around it.

The server and environment: software versions, ports and control panels exposed to the internet, external access to the database, file permissions, running as a privileged user where that isn't needed.

HTTPS and headers: a valid certificate and its automatic renewal, a forced redirect to HTTPS, and security headers that stop the page being embedded in someone else's frame and third-party code being injected into it.
