Access. Who can log in to the admin panel, the server, the repository and the hosting control panel. Accounts belonging to former employees and former contractors are a common finding, and usually an unpleasant one.

Backups. Not only "do they exist", but also "has anyone tried restoring from them" and "where are they stored". A backup available via a direct link from the site root is not protection but an extra vulnerability.

Service files and forgotten leftovers. Test subdomains, old versions of the site, configuration files, an unprotected version control folder, debug pages. Automated bots find all of these within a day of publication.

sections.heading: How an audit works
body: Reconnaissance. A map is drawn up: which technologies are used, where the entry points are, what user roles exist and which external services are connected. Without this, testing turns into random poking.

Automated scanning. Tools quickly cover the routine issues. The standard set: web vulnerability scanners such as OWASP ZAP or Burp Suite, network scanners along the lines of Nmap, checks of dependencies and the CMS for known vulnerabilities, and separate utilities for HTTPS configuration and headers.

Manual testing. The most valuable and most time-consuming part. The specialist goes through scenarios as different roles, tries to get hold of other users' data, tampers with parameters, and looks for business logic errors and for chains where two details that are harmless on their own add up to a real problem.
Infrastructure and access review: the server, permissions, backups and accounts.
Report. Findings are compiled with priorities and recommendations.
Retesting after fixes. Without it, the audit remains an exercise: you need to make sure the fix has actually closed the problem rather than masked a symptom.

sections.heading: What turns up most often
body: The same set of issues recurs from project to project, and the distribution is fairly stable.

In first place, by a wide margin, are outdated CMSs, plugins and libraries. They turn up almost every time, because updates get put off on the principle of "if it works, don't touch it". The problem is that for a publicly disclosed vulnerability a ready-made exploit is usually freely available, and such sites are found not by people but by bots that sweep the internet one address after another.
In second place is the lack of any limit on login attempts. A form that lets anyone guess passwords endlessly cancels out any password complexity policy.

Next come forgotten service files: database backups in the site root, configuration files containing passwords, an unprotected `.git` folder from which the entire source code can be downloaded, old test pages.
Then comes access to other people's data by iterating through IDs. Technically it is one unchecked line; in practice it is the ability to download other people's orders or documents.

And regularly: debug mode on the production server, accounts of former employees, passwords stored in plain text, no HTTPS on certain pages, detailed error messages that reveal the database structure.
The reassuring part: almost everything on this list can be fixed quickly and without rewriting the product. Only architectural mistakes are expensive, and they are noticeably rarer.

sections.heading: Signs that your site has already been hacked
body: A hack is by no means always noticeable. A careful attacker wants to keep access for as long as possible, so they avoid making loud changes. The following should raise a red flag.
Emails from your domain that you didn't send, or your domain suddenly landing on spam blacklists: a typical sign that the server is being used to send out spam.
An unexplained rise in load and in hosting bills. Someone else's miner or bot traffic looks exactly like this.

A browser or search engine warning that the site is unsafe, an email from your hosting provider, a sharp drop in rankings: owners often learn about a hack from exactly these, rather than from their own team.
Pages appearing that you didn't create, especially in another language or about gambling and medicines. Sometimes they are visible only to search engine crawlers and not to ordinary visitors.
Unfamiliar administrator accounts, modified files with recent dates, new jobs in the server's task scheduler.

If any of this matches, the order of action is as follows: take a fresh copy of the system in its current state (you will need it for the investigation), change all passwords and keys, including hosting and database access, check the list of administrators, and only then restore from a backup known to be clean. Restoring without finding the cause usually ends in another hack through the same door.

sections.heading: What a report should contain
body: The report is the only tangible result of an audit, and it shows the quality of the work.

Every finding is described the same way: what was found, exactly where, how to reproduce it, what risk it poses and what specifically to do. Without the "how to reproduce" step, a developer can neither verify the problem nor confirm that they have fixed it.

Severity levels are assigned according to consequences, not gut feeling: critical issues are fixed immediately, high ones within the next few days, medium ones are scheduled, and low ones are noted. They usually rely on a widely accepted vulnerability scoring scale, so that the priority can be explained rather than simply declared.
Separately, there is a short summary for management, free of jargon: how many issues were found, which of them are serious, and how long the fixes will take.
A bad report is easy to spot: it is an unprocessed scanner dump in which half the items don't apply to your site and the priorities were assigned automatically.

sections.heading: Who fixes what was found
body: A report on its own does not make anything more secure. From there, there are two paths.

The first: your own team fixes it. This is cheaper and makes more sense if you have developers who know the product. The auditor's job here is to stay available: explain anything unclear and then verify the result.

The second: whoever ran the check fixes it. This is faster and usually more reliable, because the person who found the problem understands exactly how it works. With us, this is included in the extended audit plan, while updates and ongoing checks are part of IT support.

Either way, retesting is essential. A fix that looks right often closes the symptom rather than the cause: for example, it removes the ability to enter someone else's ID in a form but leaves it open when the API is called directly.

sections.heading: The legal side
body: A data leak is not just a matter of reputation. If your site has customer accounts, enquiry forms or checkout, you are processing personal data and fall under Federal Law 152-FZ, Russia's personal data law, with all the obligations of a data operator.

Fines for violations in this area have risen many times over since 2025, and separate liability has been introduced for personal data leaks, with the amount depending on the volume of data leaked. Late notification of the regulator about an incident is penalised separately, which means that trying to deal with it quietly on your own makes your position worse.

The practical conclusion is simple: an audit costs incomparably less than the consequences of a leak, and basic hygiene (updates, restricted access, encryption, logging) is both protection and compliance with the law.

sections.heading: How to avoid needing a rescue audit
body: Security is a process, not a one-off event. Between full checks, routine work does the job, and it covers most of what we find.
Update the CMS, plugins and dependencies regularly: this removes the most widespread category of findings. When we provide IT support, we do this monthly.
Keep track of access: delete the accounts of people who have left, don't hand out administrator rights by default, and change keys after a contractor leaves.
Make backups and check at least once that you can actually restore from them. An untested backup is a hope, not a backup.
Keep an eye on the certificate, uptime and logs: most incidents first show up as an anomaly on a graph, not as a message saying "you've been hacked".
Check the site after every major release, not once a year when the occasion arises. A new feature means new entry points.

takeaways: A scanner finds what is already known, an audit finds logic and access control errors, and a pentest proves that a breach is possible. These are three different jobs.
The most widespread finding is outdated CMSs, plugins and libraries; such sites are found by bots that sweep the internet one address after another.
You need to check not only the code but also the server, access, backups and forgotten service files.
A good report explains how to reproduce the problem; otherwise a developer can neither verify it nor confirm that it has been fixed.
After fixes, retesting is needed: a fix often closes the symptom rather than the cause.
A site with customer accounts and enquiry forms processes personal data, which means it falls under 152-FZ.

razrabotka-messendzherov.title: Messenger development: how a corporate messenger works
razrabotka-messendzherov.excerpt: Your own messenger is not a window full of chats but a message delivery system. We look at the architecture, storage, encryption and deployment in a closed network, and at why companies are moving off Slack and Teams.
razrabotka-messendzherov.lead: Building a messenger today almost always means building a corporate messenger: companies are moving away from foreign services and want to keep their conversations in-house. Let's look at what such a system is made of, what is hard about it and where it makes sense to start.
razrabotka-messendzherov.metaDescription: How messengers are built: real-time delivery, storage and encryption, Active Directory, closed-network deployment, stages and budget of a corporate messenger.

sections.heading: Why a company needs its own messenger
body: Off-the-shelf services are convenient right up to the moment your conversations become an asset. Then come the questions someone else's cloud does not answer: where the messages physically sit, who has access to them, what happens if the service is switched off tomorrow, and how you explain to an inspector that your trade secrets are stored on a server in another jurisdiction.

The second motive is processes. In an ordinary messenger, conversation lives apart from the work: a request is discussed in a chat but logged in another system, and there is no link between the two. Your own messenger can be fused with your business system so that approvals, notifications about new requests and the discussion itself all end up in one place.

The third is control. An employee leaves, and you need to revoke their access but keep their correspondence. An audit arrives, and you need to pull up a discussion from the year before last. In someone else's service this is either impossible or possible only on their terms.

Hence the typical client: a company where staff correspondence is part of its trade secrets, an industry platform where communication is part of the product, or an organisation with requirements on where its data is hosted.

sections.heading: Import substitution: why companies are leaving foreign services now
body: The wave of requests for corporate messengers did not grow out of an abstract love of home-grown software. Some foreign services stopped renewing corporate subscriptions for Russian companies, some restricted features, and some simply became impossible to pay for.
For a company this is not a question of convenience but an operational risk: all internal communication hinges on a tool that can switch off without warning and without any way to export the history.

Then there is the regulatory layer. If personal data about employees or clients appears in the conversations, storing it falls under Federal Law 152-FZ, Russia's personal data law, and the requirement to host databases on Russian territory turns the choice of service into a legal question rather than a matter of taste.

The practical conclusion: a migration is almost never urgent while the service works, and it always becomes urgent the day it stops. So it is wiser to plan the move in advance, all the more so because transferring the message history is a separate task in its own right.

sections.heading: Three scenarios, not just corporate
body: "Messenger development" covers three rather different tasks, and confusing them is expensive.

A corporate messenger is for internal communication between employees. The key requirements: hosting on your own servers, roles and permissions, integration with corporate accounts, and the ability to administer and archive. Users are known in advance, so no sign-up is needed.

A chat inside a product is messaging as part of a platform: buyer and seller on a marketplace, client and contractor on a services platform, the parties to a deal. Here the users are external and strangers to one another, so moderation, complaints, protection against spam and against deals being taken off the platform come to the fore.

A client channel is how a company talks to its customers instead of through someone else's support widget. The key thing here is the conversation history, which stays with you and is linked to the client's record in your CRM.

Technically, all three share the same core: delivering and storing messages. Where they differ is in what surrounds that core: for the corporate one it is administration and security, for the product one it is moderation, for the client one it is integration with sales.

sections.heading: What a messenger is made of
body: Client apps are what the user sees: a web version, iOS and Android apps, sometimes a desktop app. They handle the interface, local storage of the history and keeping things working when the connection drops.
The server accepts messages, distributes them to recipients, stores the history, and manages users and permissions. This is the core, and it is what decides whether the system can cope with growth.
Real-time transport is the mechanism that makes a message appear for the other person immediately rather than after a page refresh.
Storage means a message database and a separate file store. Keeping them apart is a must: text conversations and attachments grow at different rates and need different handling.

Push notifications deliver messages when the app is closed. A subtle point for a corporate product: on mobile operating systems, notifications travel through the phone maker's infrastructure, so if a message is sensitive, its content is not put into the push text.
The admin side covers managing users, roles, channels and retention policies. In the corporate scenario it is the part most often underestimated, and without it the system cannot be run.

sections.heading: How a message reaches the other person
body: A persistent connection. Real-time messaging is built on WebSocket: a channel that stays open, so the server can push data into it on its own without waiting for a request. Where the connection is unstable, fallback mechanisms and smart reconnection are added.

Queues and acknowledgements. A message does not count as delivered until the recipient has confirmed it. Hence the familiar ticks: sent, delivered, read. Behind them is not interface decoration but a protocol that guarantees a message is not lost if the connection breaks halfway.

Ordering and duplicates. Two non-obvious problems that surface under real load. Messages can arrive in a different order from the one they were sent in, and when resent after a dropped connection they can be duplicated. This is solved with client-side identifiers and server-side numbering, and it has to be built in from the start: reworking it later is painful.
Working offline. The app must be able to accept a message, show it as unsent and deliver it once the connection is back. For a mobile client this is a mandatory part, not an enhancement.

Calls. Audio and video run over WebRTC, and where possible the traffic goes directly between devices. But "where possible" means that on a corporate network with a strict firewall you will need a relay server, and it has to be planned for in advance.

sections.heading: Storage and encryption
body: Transport encryption is the mandatory minimum: the channel between client and server is protected, and the conversation cannot be intercepted in transit. It is everywhere and is not up for discussion.

End-to-end encryption is another story. With it, messages are decrypted only on the participants' devices, and the server physically cannot read the conversation. It sounds like an unqualified good, but for a corporate system it is a trade-off, not an upgrade.

The thing is, along with the ability to read conversations the server loses everything else: server-side search through the history, an archive for audits and investigations, history recovery when a device is lost, moderation. A company that is obliged to retain business correspondence cannot do so with end-to-end encryption.

That is why corporate products usually opt for a middle ground: channel encryption and storage encryption, role-based access, logging of data access, and end-to-end encryption applied selectively, for particular private chats where it is genuinely needed.

The answer to "so what is the right way?" depends not on technology but on whom you have to trust and whom you answer to. This is worth talking through before development starts, because reworking the storage architecture later is the most expensive change of all.

sections.heading: Integrations you cannot do without
body: Corporate accounts. An employee should not have to create yet another password: sign-in goes through the existing user directory, whether Active Directory, LDAP or corporate SSO. This also settles the question of people leaving: access is revoked in one place.

Notifications from internal systems. The most underrated feature, and at the same time the one that pays off best: a request from your business system, an order status or a contract approval arrives in the chat where people already are, not in the email they open twice a day.
Bots and scenarios. Automatic answers to routine internal questions, on-call alerts, taking in support requests.
A link to the CRM in the client scenario: the conversation is attached to the client's record, and the manager sees the whole history, not just the last three messages.

It is the integrations that usually decide whether the system takes root. Employees have no use for a messenger that merely repeats what WhatsApp already does: people go back to the familiar tool within a month. The one that takes root is the one that has something the others do not.

sections.heading: Where it all gets deployed
body: The cloud. Quick and cheap to start with, and suited to product scenarios with no requirements on where data is hosted.
Your own server. The default compromise for the corporate case: the data stays with you, the infrastructure is clear, and maintenance is handled by you or by a contractor.

A closed network. The system runs on a network with no internet access. This is the strictest option, and it changes the whole project: updates have to be delivered manually, external services are unavailable, and mobile push notifications in their usual form are impossible, so they are replaced by mechanisms of your own. If a closed network is in the requirements, it needs to be raised at the first meeting, not halfway through development.

sections.heading: Where to start and what not to do straight away
body: A messenger is best built in iterations, and the first version should be boring: one-to-one and group chats, sending text and files, notifications, a web interface. That is enough for people to start using it and for you to see what they actually lack.

What people almost always ask for at the start and what is almost always worth postponing: video calls, end-to-end encryption, desktop apps, complex access rights, bots. Each of these is expensive, and almost none of them gets used in the first version.

What cannot be postponed, because reworking it after the fact costs more: the message storage scheme, the mechanism for ordering and duplicates, the model of roles and permissions, and the sign-in method. This is the foundation.

And, separately, migrating the history from the old service. The task looks like a technical trifle, but in practice it turns out to be comparable in scope to building a separate feature, especially if the old service exports its data in an awkward format.

sections.heading: Timelines and budget
body: A first working version (chats, channels, a web interface, accounts and roles) takes about a month and a half and costs from {price:200000}.
A version you can use in earnest, with file sharing, iOS and Android mobile clients, integrations with internal systems and administration: two to three months, from {price:300000}.
A system in a closed network with higher resilience requirements and planned ongoing development: from four months and from {price:500000}.

Three things affect the estimate most: the number of platforms (each mobile client is a separate piece of work), how strict the hosting and security requirements are, and the number of systems it has to work with. We keep current packages and the scope of work on the service page.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
body: Trying to copy Telegram. Competing with a product that has thousands of person-years invested in it is pointless and unnecessary: the value of a corporate messenger lies not in a wealth of features but in the fact that it is yours and knows your processes.
Leaving administration for later. A system without user and permission management cannot be operated, and bolting it onto a running product is awkward.
Forgetting about migrating the history and about training people. A technically flawless messenger that nobody has been moved onto stays empty.
Choosing end-to-end encryption by default without checking whether it conflicts with your own requirements for retaining correspondence.
And the most common one: launching everything at once. A project that spends six months being built "in full" comes out just as half the requirements have gone out of date.

takeaways: Demand for in-house messengers today is mostly corporate: moving off foreign services and requirements on where data is hosted.
All scenarios share the same core, delivering and storing messages; they differ in administration, moderation and integrations.
Message ordering, duplicates, the storage scheme and the permissions model are built in from the start, since reworking them costs the most.
End-to-end encryption deprives the server of search, an archive and moderation, so in a corporate system it is a trade-off, not an upgrade.
The messenger that takes root is the one with something the familiar ones lack: notifications and requests from internal systems.
The first version should be boring: chats, files, notifications, web. Calls and encryption are almost always worth postponing.

parsing-dannyh.title: Data parsing: files, databases and websites
parsing-dannyh.excerpt: Parsing isn't just collecting data from websites. We look at how Excel, PDF and log files are read, how data is pulled out of other people's databases, what to do about protected sources and what it all costs.
parsing-dannyh.lead: The word "parsing" covers three different jobs: breaking down a file, pulling data out of someone else's database and collecting information from a website. They have one thing in common: the data sits in an awkward form and you need it in a usable one. We'll go through all three, with examples of what usually breaks.
parsing-dannyh.metaTitle: Data parsing: files, databases and websites
parsing-dannyh.metaDescription: What data parsing is and how it works: CSV, Excel, XML, JSON and PDF files, database extraction, web scraping, tools, legal limits, timelines and cost.

sections.heading: What parsing is and why a business needs it
body: Parsing (literally, breaking something down into its parts) is the automatic conversion of data from an awkward format into a usable one. A parser reads the source, finds the fragments you need, brings them to a single format and puts them where they can be worked with: a spreadsheet, a database or a CRM.

The key word here is "automatic". You can do the same job by hand: open the supplier's price list, copy the item name, find it in your own system, type in the new price. With a hundred items that's an evening. With a hundred thousand it's a job that simply cannot be done: by the time you reach the end of the catalogue, the prices at the start will already be out of date.

Hence the typical reasons: filling a catalogue from supplier price lists, updating prices and stock levels daily, moving data from an old system to a new one, combining exports from several sources into one report, monitoring the market. Wherever data arrives regularly and in someone else's format, a parser replaces not a programmer but the person who used to copy cells.

sections.heading: Parsing files: CSV, Excel, XML, JSON, PDF
body: The most common kind, and also the most underestimated. Reading an Excel file looks like a five-minute job, and for a tidy file that's true. The problems start when the file was made by a person.

CSV is plain text with delimiters. The pitfalls: the delimiter may be a semicolon or a tab rather than a comma; the same characters turn up inside values; line breaks hide in the middle of a field. It is read with the language's standard tools or with pandas, which handles most dialects on its own.

Excel (XLSX, XLS) is the most temperamental format, because it isn't a data table but a canvas to draw on. Merged cells, a header spread over three rows, a product and its SKU on different levels, numbers saved as text, blank separator rows between sections. It is parsed with openpyxl or pandas, but most of the work goes not into reading but into restoring the structure the author kept in their head.

XML and JSON were designed for machines, and they are usually the easiest: the structure is stated explicitly. XML is read with lxml, JSON with the language's standard tools. The difficulty comes with large volumes: a file of several gigabytes can't be loaded into memory in one go, so it is parsed as a stream, one element at a time.

PDF is a format for printing, not for data. It has no rows or columns, only characters with coordinates on the page. A table is "visible" to a human only because the characters are lined up. Libraries such as pdfplumber and PyMuPDF rebuild the structure from those coordinates, and on tidy documents this works well.

DBF is a legacy of FoxPro and old accounting systems, and it still turns up in data exchange with accounting and the warehouse. It is read with specialised libraries; the main difficulty is the encoding, which we cover below.
Logs are text files whose lines all follow one format. They are parsed with regular expressions, and the main work here is not reading but aggregation: counting, grouping, finding anomalies.

sections.heading: What usually breaks when parsing files
body: Encodings. Russian text in old exports comes in CP1251 or CP866, while the program expects UTF-8 by default, and the output is mojibake, garbled characters. It's worse when the encoding changes from file to file: then it is detected automatically, with libraries such as chardet, and you still keep the option of setting it by hand, because auto-detection gets short strings wrong.

Merged cells in Excel. To a person, a merged cell means "this heading applies to all the rows below". To a program it is one value in the first cell and nothing in all the others. You have to restore the logic: carry the value down to the next filled cell, and tell a section heading from a product row.

Scans instead of text in PDF. The document looks like a table, but inside it is an image. No text-parsing library will help here; you need OCR, recognition with Tesseract or cloud services. That is a fundamentally different level of reliability: recognition makes mistakes with digits, confuses zero with the letter O, and the result always has to be checked. If the supplier has the same price list in Excel, it's cheaper to ask for it than to recognise a scan.

We have met all of these cases on real projects, and they lead to one conclusion: the time goes not into reading the format but into handling exceptions. That's why we always give an estimate after we've looked at the real files, not at a description of them.

sections.heading: Parsing databases
body: The second big kind is when the data sits not in a file but in someone else's database or an outdated one. There are three types of task here.

Migration. A company is moving from an old system to a new one, and the data has to be transferred: customers, orders, products, history. The difficulty is that the structures don't match: what was one field in the old database is split into three in the new one, and reference data has to be matched by hand.

Exports for reports. The data exists, but you can't get at it through the interface: you need a slice the system can't produce. The parser queries the database directly, collects what's needed and passes it to a report or a BI system.

Synchronisation. Two systems must see the same data: for example, warehouse stock in the accounting system and stock levels on the website. This is no longer a one-off export but a regular exchange with conflict handling: what to do if a record has changed in both systems.

In practice we have worked with PostgreSQL, MySQL, MS SQL Server, SQLite and databases of 1C, Russia's most widespread accounting platform. Technically, connecting to any of them is routine; all the difficulty lies in understanding someone else's schema. Table names like SC1247 and field names like SP2891 are normal for 1C, and working out a structure like that takes longer than the export itself.

sections.heading: When you aren't given access to the database
body: A common situation: you need the data, but there is no direct access to the database. The system's owner isn't prepared to open it up to the outside, the contractor who built it can't be reached, or the licence simply doesn't allow external connections.

Then you work through whatever is available. If the system can export reports, you parse the exports, and the task comes down to the file parsing covered above. If there is an API, even an undocumented one, you use it. As a last resort the data is taken through the web interface: the program logs in under an account with legitimate access and goes through the same screens a person would.

The last option works, but it is the most fragile: it breaks with any update to the interface. We warn about this in advance and suggest it only when the other routes are closed, and at the same time we advise you to negotiate proper access after all, because it is cheaper to maintain.

sections.heading: Parsing websites
body: The third kind is collecting data from web pages. Here the source doesn't hand you a file, and the structure has to be extracted from the markup.

The simple case: the server returns ready-made HTML. The parser loads the page with an HTTP client, parses the markup with BeautifulSoup or lxml and pulls out the data by selectors: "the price is in this block with this class". For large projects with hundreds of thousands of pages, the Scrapy framework is used: it manages the request queue, concurrency and retries itself.

The hard case: the page is assembled in the browser. The server returns an empty shell, and the content is loaded by scripts. Then a headless browser is used, Playwright or Selenium: it actually opens the page, waits for it to load and returns the final markup. This is slower and needs more resources, so it is used when the simple route doesn't work.

It's also worth checking whether the source has an official API. It is almost always faster, more stable and more legitimate than parsing the markup, and it's the first thing we check when we take on a job.

sections.heading: What to do if the source is closed to collection
body: Websites protect themselves from mass collection: they limit request rates, show a CAPTCHA, require a login, block by IP address. That is the owner's legal right: they pay for the servers and are entitled to decide who uses them.

Our position here is simple, and we talk it through with the client at the start. A well-behaved parser acts like a polite guest: it pauses between requests, creates no more load than an ordinary visitor, identifies itself honestly in its headers, respects robots.txt and doesn't go behind a login without the owner's permission. With this approach most sources can be collected without any tricks: blocks are usually triggered by aggressive collection, not careful collection.

If, however, the source is deliberately closed (there's a CAPTCHA, access is for customers only, the terms of use explicitly forbid it), we say so plainly rather than start getting around the protection. Circumventing technical protection measures moves the task out of development and into legal risk, and the risk is the client's: it is the client who is later answerable for the collected data.

Instead, we offer routes that work: ask the owner for official access or an export (this works more often than people think); find the same data in an open source or from an aggregator; buy a ready-made dataset. Clients sometimes don't like this answer in the moment. But a project that runs into a block or a legal claim a month later costs more than an honest "we can't take this source, let's look for another one".

sections.heading: Parsing search queries
body: On the Russian-language internet, "parsing" has one more meaning: collecting search queries, that is, keyword research. The technique is similar, but the purpose is different: what you collect is not products but what people search for.

The sources here are query statistics services such as Yandex Wordstat, the keyword tool of Russia's main search engine, along with search suggestions and ready-made keyword databases. The output is a list of phrases with search volumes, which is used to build the site structure and plan content.

Most of these services have official APIs, and working through them is the right way rather than scraping the interface: it doesn't breach the terms of use and doesn't break when the site is redesigned. To be honest, this is more an SEO task than a development one, and we take it on as part of larger projects rather than as a separate service.

sections.heading: Why parsers break and how to prevent it
body: A parser is just about the only kind of program that breaks not because something was changed in it, but because something changed outside it. The supplier changed the header in the price list, the website updated its layout, a new field appeared in the database, and collection that worked yesterday returns nothing today or, worse, rubbish.

You can't avoid this entirely, but you can make sure a breakdown isn't a disaster. The first measure is checking the result on the way in, not on the way out. The parser knows what to expect: if forty rows arrive from a price list of ten thousand, if a price turns negative, if half the columns disappear, it stops and reports the problem instead of loading corrupted data into the production database.

The second is alerts. A silent failure is worse than a loud one: the data quietly goes stale, and you find out a week later from a customer complaint. So the parser logs every run to monitoring and sends a notification to Telegram or by email if something goes wrong.

The third is anchoring to meaning, not position. A column in Excel is found by its header name, not its number; data on a page is found by stable attributes, not by a long chain of nesting that will break with any design change.
The fourth is keeping the source material. Downloaded files and pages are stored as they are, so when something fails you can see exactly what changed. Without this you are debugging blind.
The fifth is graceful degradation. If one optional field out of twenty fails to parse, it is better to write the other nineteen and flag the gap than to bring down the whole export.

sections.heading: Legal limits
body: Collecting publicly available data is lawful in itself, but there are limits, and it's worth knowing them before you start.

Personal data. Names, phone numbers, addresses and email addresses are personal data under Federal Law 152-FZ, Russia's personal data law, even if they are publicly available. Collecting them makes you a personal data operator, with all the obligations that follow. The rule is simple: if the task can be solved without personal data, solve it without.

Copyright. Texts, photographs and descriptions are protected by copyright regardless of how you obtained them. Collecting someone else's product descriptions for internal analytics and publishing them on your own website are fundamentally different things in the eyes of the law.

Terms of use and robots.txt. A robots.txt file isn't a legal document, but it expresses the owner's wishes, and ignoring it becomes an argument against you. A website's user agreement may explicitly prohibit automated collection, and that is already a contractual matter.
Load. Collection that interferes with someone else's service is a separate story, and it is closer to unlawful interference than to harmless reading of public pages.

The practical conclusion: collect only what the task really needs, don't touch personal data without a legal basis, don't publish other people's content as your own, and don't create load. In borderline cases it's cheaper to show the task to a lawyer than to sort things out afterwards.

sections.heading: How much it costs and how long it takes
body: The cost of a parser is determined not by the volume of data but by the number of exceptions. Collecting a million rows from tidy XML is easier and cheaper than collecting a thousand from a dozen messy Excel files with different structures.

Our guide figures are these. A simple parser with one source and export to a spreadsheet: from {price:50000}. A system with several sources, automatic scheduled collection and export to a database or CRM: from {price:110000}. Complex cases with protected sources, a resilient architecture and monitoring: from {price:220000}.

As for timelines: a simple parser usually takes one to two weeks, regular collection from several sources two to four weeks, and a large system with monitoring from a month and a half. Most of this time goes not into code but into working through exceptions in the real data.

What affects the price most: the number of sources and the variety of their formats; whether a headless browser is needed; how dirty the source data is; whether reference data has to be matched; how often it updates and what reliability is required. That's why we don't name a figure from a description of the task: first we look at the real files or pages, and only then do we estimate.

And a fair warning: a parser needs ongoing support. Sources change, and every few months something has to be fixed. A one-off build without support is a saving that ends with the data quietly ceasing to update six months later.

sections.heading: Example: a catalogue of 100,000 items
body: One of our projects was an online shop selling spare parts for heavy machinery. The task was to fill the catalogue: around a hundred thousand items from the supplier, with part numbers, specifications, prices and the machine assemblies they belong to.

There's no way to do this by hand: even at one minute per item it comes to more than a year of one person's work. We collected the data automatically, brought part numbers and names to a single format, matched the product range against the internal reference data and set up regular price and stock updates, so the catalogue wouldn't go out of date the day after launch.

The main work, as usual, was not in collection but in normalisation: the same product had different names at the supplier and at the client, some specifications were written into the general text description, and some part numbers differed only in letter case and spaces.
The result is a catalogue in which customers find the part they need themselves, instead of phoning to check availability.

sections.heading: How we work
body: We start with real data: we ask you to send sample files, access to a test database or links to the pages. We don't give an estimate based on a description of the task: too often the description and the actual content differ.

Next we design: which fields are needed, how to match them with your reference data, how often to update, where to export, what to do if something fails. Then we build and launch collection with monitoring, so you hear about a problem from the system rather than from a customer.
We deliver the result where it is used: a spreadsheet, a database, a CRM or an API exchange with your system, with no manual copying in between.

takeaways: Parsing covers three different jobs: breaking down files, extracting data from databases and collecting it from websites.
The time goes not into reading the format but into handling exceptions: broken encodings, merged cells, scans instead of text.
If a source has an API or an official export, it is always better than parsing the markup.
We don't get around anti-collection protection: if a source is deliberately closed, we look for a legal route to the same data.
A parser must check its results and report failures: a silent breakdown is worse than a loud one.
Personal data falls under 152-FZ even when it is publicly available.
